evidence: All six classes (AddTaskToProjectUseCase, AssignTaskUseCase, CreateProjectUseCase, CreateUserUseCase, ListProjectTasksUseCase, MarkTaskDoneUseCase) implement UseCase<I, O> from '../ports/UseCase'
AddTaskToProjectUseCase.ts and ListProjectTasksUseCase.ts both call parseTaskStatus from domain/value-objects/TaskStatus instead of re-implementing status validation
AssignTaskUseCase.ts calls task.assignTo(user) and MarkTaskDoneUseCase.ts calls task.markDone(), so the state-change rules stay in the domain entity
Output mapping always goes through the shared mappers toTaskDto, toProjectDto and toUserDto from ../dto
ID generation always goes through the IdGenerator port (this.ids.next()) in the Create* use cases and AddTaskToProjectUseCase
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All six files cover one concern: application use cases that coordinate domain entities through repository ports. They follow the same shape throughout. Each class implements UseCase<Input, Output> and receives its dependencies (repositories and IdGenerator) through the constructor. Each loads or creates entities, hands the business behaviour to domain methods (Task.create, Project.create, User.create, task.assignTo, task.markDone), saves through the repository, and returns the result through the shared DTO mappers (toTaskDto, toProjectDto, toUserDto). No file goes around these abstractions. None works on persistence directly or builds DTOs inline. Rules and invariants stay in one place each. Status parsing goes to the domain's parseTaskStatus. Due-date validation goes to DueDate.fromIso. The rules for assigning and completing tasks live in domain entity methods. The repeated 'findById then throw NotFoundError' guard is the same small orchestration step in several files. It does not copy a business invariant, because the error type itself lives in the domain. One small style difference: CreateProjectInput comes from ProjectDto, while task inputs come from TaskInputs. Those files are outside this unit, and the difference does not break cohesion.
